Following parturition, the suckling juvenile experiences rapid somatic growth, with the wet weight at weaning having been recorded at 3900 grams [Wwx = 3900 grams]. The sholder-rump length at weaning, a key metric of skeletal development during the nursing stage, is documented at 28.8 cm . This protracted period of maternal investment, characterized by the ongoing provision of milk during the suckling stage, is relatively long compared to many cercopithecines of similar body size and likely reflects the high metabolic demands placed on the infant prior to achieving nutritional independence through the dietary transition to solid food.

Sexual maturation in male geladas proceeds along a distinct trajectory compared to females. The corresponding sholder-rump length at puberty for females is substantially smaller, at 43.5 cm [Lp = 43.5 cm]. This pronounced sexual dimorphism in the timing of gonadal maturation is a hallmark of the species' polygynous social system, where males delay reproductive maturation while continuing to grow, likely in preparation for future competition over access to females.

Adult body mass in Theropithecus gelada is strongly dimorphic, a trait that underlies their complex multi-level social organization. The ultimate wet weight for female geladas reaches approximately 11000 grams [Wwi = approximately 11000 grams], a relatively modest size for a terrestrial Old World monkey. In contrast, the ultimate wet weight for male individuals is considerably greater, attaining about 18500 grams [Wwi = about 18500 grams]. This nearly 1.7-fold difference in mass is reflected in the ultimate sholder-rump length, which for females peaks at around 49 cm [Li = around 49 cm], while the ultimate sholder-rump length form males is substantially larger at 56.3 cm [Li = 56.3 cm]. This pronounced sexual dimorphism in both mass and linear skeletal dimensions is tightly linked to the intense male-male competition observed in gelada reproductive units, where larger body size confers a significant advantage in establishing and maintaining dominance within the hierarchical social system.

Reproductive output in geladas is characterized by a slow life-history pace typical of large-bodied terrestrial primates. Under the stable thermoregulatory conditions afforded by their high-altitude environment, where core body temperature is maintained at 38 °C [T = 38 °C], the gestation time is 168 days [tg = 168 days]. This represents a comparatively short intrauterine developmental period for a primate of this adult body mass. Following parturition, females exhibit a single offspring per birth event [N_R_i = single offspring per birth event], with inter-birth intervals resulting in less than one reproductive event annually [F_R_i = one reproductive event annually]. This exceptionally low reproductive rate, which represents a daily fecundity far below that of most comparably-sized mammals, is consistent with the species' reliance on the predictable but sparse grass resources of the Ethiopian highlands. Such slow reproductive pacing is thought to allow mothers to allocate sufficient time and energy to each dependent newborn during the prolonged nursing stage essential for infant survival.

Longevity in geladas is considerable, reflecting their position among the slower-living primate species. At the typical core temperature of 38 °C [T = 38 °C], the maximum lifespan for the species has been documented at approximately 36 years [am = approximately 36 years], placing them among the longest-lived members of the tribe Papionini. This extended lifespan is consistent with the species' delayed life history, where first reproduction occurs only after a prolonged period of somatic growth and social maturation. The slow pace of life is further evidenced by the relatively modest maximum reproductive rate, with females producing approximately one offspring every two years, a rate that ultimately results from the combination of singleton births and lengthy inter-birth intervals. Comparative analyses with related baboon species suggest that the gelada's reliance on a low-quality, graminivorous diet in the resource-limited alpine meadows of the Simien Mountains has favored extended longevity and reduced annual fecundity as strategies for buffering against environmental stochasticity.
